fallacies.name: Ad Hominem
fallacies.description: Attacking the person making an argument rather than addressing the argument itself
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when someone responds to an argument by attacking the character, motive, or other attribute of the person making the argument, rather than addressing the substance of the argument itself.
examples: You can't trust John's opinion on climate change because he's not a scientist
She's just saying that because she's young and inexperienced

fallacies.name: Strawman
fallacies.description: Misrepresenting someone's argument to make it easier to attack
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy involves distorting, exaggerating, or oversimplifying someone's position to make it easier to refute, rather than addressing their actual argument.
examples: So you're saying we should just let criminals run free?
You want to destroy the economy for a few trees?

fallacies.name: False Dilemma
fallacies.description: Presenting only two options when more alternatives exist
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when someone presents a situation as having only two possible outcomes or choices, when in reality there are more options available.
examples: You're either with us or against us
We must choose between freedom and security

fallacies.name: Slippery Slope
fallacies.description: Arguing that one event will lead to a chain of negative consequences
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy assumes that if one thing happens, it will inevitably lead to a series of other (usually bad) things happening, without adequate evidence for this chain of causation.
examples: If we allow this, next thing you know...
This is just the beginning, soon they'll...

fallacies.name: Appeal to Authority
fallacies.description: Using an authority's opinion as evidence when the authority is not expert in that field
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when someone cites an authority figure to support their argument, but the authority is not actually an expert in the relevant field or their expertise is irrelevant.
examples: Einstein said this about politics, so it must be true
A famous actor endorses this product, so it must work

fallacies.name: Bandwagon
fallacies.description: Arguing that something is true because many people believe it
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy assumes that because many people believe something or do something, it must be correct or the right thing to do.
examples: Everyone knows that...
Most people agree that...

fallacies.name: Red Herring
fallacies.description: Introducing irrelevant information to distract from the main issue
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy involves introducing irrelevant material to the issue being discussed, so that everyone's attention is diverted away from the points being made.
examples: Why worry about the environment when there are homeless people?
Instead of discussing the budget, let's talk about education

fallacies.name: Circular Reasoning
fallacies.description: Using the conclusion as evidence for the conclusion
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when the conclusion of an argument is used as a premise of that same argument; in other words, the argument assumes what it is trying to prove.
examples: The Bible is true because it says so in the Bible
He's trustworthy because he's honest

fallacies.name: Hasty Generalization
fallacies.description: Drawing broad conclusions from limited examples
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy involves making a generalized conclusion about a whole group or class based on a small sample, often just one or two examples.
examples: I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there must be rude
This product broke after one day, so the company makes terrible products

fallacies.name: False Cause
fallacies.description: Assuming that because B comes after A, A caused B
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy assumes that because one thing happened before another, the first thing must have caused the second (correlation implies causation).
examples: I wore my lucky shirt and we won the game, so my shirt caused the victory
Crime decreased after the new law, so the law caused the decrease

fallacies.name: Appeal to Emotion
fallacies.description: Using emotional manipulation instead of logical reasoning
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy attempts to win an argument by exploiting people's emotions rather than using logical reasoning and evidence.
examples: Think of the children!
If you really cared about America...

fallacies.name: Tu Quoque
fallacies.description: Avoiding criticism by pointing out the critic's hypocrisy
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when someone responds to criticism by pointing out that the critic is also guilty of the same thing, rather than addressing the criticism itself.
examples: You can't criticize my driving when you speed too
Look who's talking about being late!

fallacies.name: No True Scotsman
fallacies.description: Moving the goalposts to exclude counterexamples
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy involves making a universal statement, then when presented with a counterexample, modifying the original statement to exclude the counterexample.
examples: No true Christian would do that
Real Americans support this policy

fallacies.name: Loaded Question
fallacies.description: Asking a question that contains a controversial assumption
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy involves asking a question that contains a controversial or unjustified assumption, forcing the person to accept the assumption in order to answer.
examples: When did you stop cheating on your taxes?
Why are you so selfish?

fallacies.name: Begging the Question
fallacies.description: Assuming the conclusion in the premises
fallacies.explanation: This fallacy occurs when an argument's premises assume the truth of the conclusion, instead of supporting it.
examples: Murder is wrong because killing people is immoral
This law is just because it's the right thing to do
